items.title: 14.4.6 Applications of Vectors in Real World

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The products of vectors are not only about geometry. This section shows three everyday uses: the cross product gives torque (Example 29), the magnitude of a vector gives the size of a force (Example 30), and the dot product gives total revenue (Example 31).

blocks.title: Example 29
blocks.problem: A plumber exerts a force of 30 pounds along the negative \(y\)-axis on a lever connected to a machine. The pivot point of the lever is at the origin \((0, 0, 0)\), and the force is applied at the point \((1.2\text{ ft}, 0.5\text{ ft}, 0\text{ ft})\). Determine the torque produced by this force about the pivot point.
steps:
Given: force of magnitude 30 pounds along the negative \(y\)-axis; pivot at \(O(0, 0, 0)\); force applied at \((1.2, 0.5, 0)\) (in feet).
To find: the torque \(\underline{\tau}\) about the pivot.
Method: torque is \(\underline{\tau} = \underline{r}\times \underline{F}\) (Key Concept), where \(\underline{r}\) runs from the pivot to the point where the force acts. Compute the cross product with the determinant formula.

Step 1: Position vector
\[\underline{r} = 1.2\underline{i} + 0.5\underline{j} + 0\underline{k}\]
Why: the pivot is the origin, so \(\underline{r}\) is just the position vector of \((1.2, 0.5, 0)\).

Step 2: Force vector
\[\underline{F} = 0\underline{i} - 30\underline{j} + 0\underline{k}\]
Why: the force has magnitude 30 and points along the negative \(y\)-axis (downward), so only the \(\underline{j}\)-component is non-zero and it is negative.

Step 3: Set up the cross product
\[\underline{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 1.2 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & -30 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: determinant formula of the cross product: row 1 the unit vectors, row 2 the components of \(\underline{r}\), row 3 those of \(\underline{F}\). The order matters: \(\underline{r}\times \underline{F}\), not \(\underline{F}\times \underline{r}\).

Step 4: Expand
\[= \underline{i}\big[(0.5)(0) - (0)(-30)\big]\]
\[- \underline{j}\big[(1.2)(0) - (0)(0)\big]\]
\[+ \underline{k}\big[(1.2)(-30) - (0.5)(0)\big]\]
\[= 0\underline{i} - 0\underline{j} - 36\underline{k}\]
Why: each unit vector multiplies the \(2\times 2\) determinant left after deleting its column; the \(\underline{j}\) term has a minus sign.

Step 5: State the torque
\[\underline{\tau} = -36\underline{k}\ \text{pound-feet}\]
Why: the torque has magnitude 36 and points along the negative \(z\)-axis.

Check: the force is along the \(y\)-axis, so only the part of \(\underline{r}\) across it, \(1.2\) ft along \(x\), turns the lever: \(30\times 1.2 = 36\). Direction: \(\underline{i}\times(-\underline{j}) = -\underline{k}\), the negative \(z\)-direction. Both agree.
blocks.answer: \(\underline{\tau} = -36\underline{k}\) pound-feet. Thus, the torque is 36 feet-pounds in the negative \(z\)-direction.

blocks.title: Key Concept
blocks.text:
Torque measures the turning (rotational) effect of a force applied to an object about a pivot point. It is found by taking the cross product of the position vector \(\underline{r}\) (which runs from the pivot point to the point where the force is applied) and the force vector \(\underline{F}\) itself.
Mathematically, \(\underline{\tau} = \underline{r}\times \underline{F}\).

blocks.alt: A wrench turning a hexagonal bolt. The position vector r runs along the handle from the bolt (the pivot) to the end of the handle, where the force F is applied at an angle theta to the extension of r. The torque vector tau points along the axis of the bolt.
blocks.caption: Figure: torque on a wrench, τ = r × F (original drawing after the textbook's Key Concept figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Torque is what makes things turn: a spanner turning a nut, a door turning on its hinges, a plumber's lever. A larger force, or the same force applied further from the pivot, turns more easily; that is why a long spanner helps. \(|\underline{\tau}| = |\underline{r}||\underline{F}|\sin\theta\), so a force pointing straight along the handle (\(\theta = 0\)) does not turn it at all.
Units: force in pounds times distance in feet. The book writes "pound-feet" in one line and "feet-pounds" in the next; both name the same unit (lb·ft).

blocks.title: Example 30
blocks.problem: During a building construction, a crane exerts a force to pull a concrete block, represented by the vector \(\underline{F} = [4500, 3300, 2140]\) Newton. Each component corresponds to the force exerted along the \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) axes, respectively. What is the magnitude of this force?
steps:
Given: \(\underline{F} = [4500, 3300, 2140]\) N, i.e. \(\underline{F} = 4500\underline{i} + 3300\underline{j} + 2140\underline{k}\).
To find: the magnitude \(|\underline{F}|\).
Method: the magnitude of a vector in space is \(\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}\) (14.1).

Step 1: Write the formula
\[|\underline{F}| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{4500^{2} + 3300^{2} + 2140^{2}}\]
Why: the three components are perpendicular to one another, so the length is found by Pythagoras in three dimensions.

Step 2: Square each component
\[4500^{2} = 20250000\]
\[3300^{2} = 10890000\]
\[2140^{2} = 4579600\]
Why: work out each square separately before adding, to avoid slips with the zeros.

Step 3: Add and take the square root
\[20250000 + 10890000 + 4579600\]
\[= 35719600\]
\[|\underline{F}| = \sqrt{35719600}\]
\[\approx 5976.59\]
Why: the square root of the sum is the magnitude; it is not a perfect square, so we round to two decimal places.
Check: \(5976.59^{2} \approx 35719628\), very close to \(35719600\). Also the magnitude must exceed the largest component \(4500\) and be less than the sum \(9940\); \(5976.59\) does.
blocks.answer: The magnitude of the force exerted by the crane is approximately \(5976.59\) Newton.

blocks.title: Example 31
blocks.problem: The components of \(\underline{u} = 300\underline{i} + 250\underline{j} + 180\underline{k}\) represent the respective number of jackets, shoes, and handbags sold at a store. The components of \(\underline{v} = 3500\underline{i} + 4200\underline{j} + 6840\underline{k}\) represent the respective prices (in rupees) per unit for each product. Find \(\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v}\) and explain what the result tells us in real life.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 300\underline{i} + 250\underline{j} + 180\underline{k}\) (numbers sold of jackets, shoes, handbags) and \(\underline{v} = 3500\underline{i} + 4200\underline{j} + 6840\underline{k}\) (price per item in rupees).
To find: \(\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v}\) and its meaning.
Method: dot product in components: multiply matching components and add (14.2).

Step 1: Write the dot product
\[\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v} = (300\underline{i} + 250\underline{j} + 180\underline{k})\]
\[\cdot\,(3500\underline{i} + 4200\underline{j} + 6840\underline{k})\]
Why: the dot product pairs the \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) components.

Step 2: Multiply matching components
\[(300)(3500) = 1{,}050{,}000\]
\[(250)(4200) = 1{,}050{,}000\]
\[(180)(6840) = 1{,}231{,}200\]
Why: each product is (number sold) \(\times\) (price), i.e. the money earned from one kind of item.

Step 3: Add
\[\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v} = 1{,}050{,}000 + 1{,}050{,}000 + 1{,}231{,}200\]
\[= 3{,}331{,}200\]
Why: the dot product is the sum of the three products.

Step 4: Meaning in real life
Jackets bring Rs. 1,050,000, shoes Rs. 1,050,000 and handbags Rs. 1,231,200; the dot product adds them, so it is the total revenue (total money received from sales).
Why: quantity times price is revenue, and the dot product is exactly 'multiply pairwise and add'.
Check: rough estimate \(300\times 3500 \approx 1\) million, \(250\times 4200 \approx 1\) million, \(180\times 6840 \approx 1.2\) million; total about \(3.3\) million. Matches.
blocks.answer: \(\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v} = 3{,}331{,}200\). The result tells us that total revenue generated from selling all the three product is Rs. 3,331,200.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "selling all the three product". It should read "selling all the three products".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Torque: \(\underline{\tau} = \underline{r}\times \underline{F}\), with \(\underline{r}\) from the pivot to the point where the force acts.
2. Magnitude of \(\underline{F} = [x, y, z]\): \(|\underline{F}| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}\).
3. Quantities \(\cdot\) prices (dot product) = total revenue.
4. Always state the units and the direction of a vector answer.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Computing \(\underline{F}\times \underline{r}\) instead of \(\underline{r}\times \underline{F}\): the sign of the torque reverses.
2. Writing the force along the negative \(y\)-axis as \(+30\underline{j}\).
3. Answering Example 31 with a vector: a dot product is a number.
